nodes.question: Which metrics should you use to measure demand forecast quality, and why is MAPE bad for retail? When should you use WAPE/bias?
nodes.answer: MAPE = mean relative error, but it's bad for retail: it blows up on items with low/zero demand (division by ~0) and overweights small SKUs. WAPE (volume-weighted absolute error) is more robust — it weights the error by actual sales and reflects the impact on the business. Bias (ME) shows systematic deviation: persistent under-forecasting → shortages on the shelf, over-forecasting → write-offs/frozen working capital. In practice people look at a combination: WAPE (accuracy by volume) + bias (direction of the error) + segmentation by ABC/turnover rate. MAPE alone as the only metric for retail is an anti-pattern.
nodes.title: Demand forecast metrics

nodes.question: Why do you need data lineage (OpenLineage), and how do you quickly pinpoint a broken data mart in an Airflow → Spark → Trino → ClickHouse chain?
nodes.answer: Lineage records which datasets each job reads/writes (input→output), building a data dependency graph. OpenLineage is an open event standard; it integrates with Airflow/Spark, and the events are collected in Marquez/a data catalog. The benefit: during an incident you can see which upstream task broke the data mart and which downstream consumers will be affected (impact analysis), without manually digging through DAGs. Pinpointing a broken data mart: follow the lineage up the graph to the nearest job whose run failed/whose DQ metric dropped (freshness, row volume, non-null), and match the incident time against the runs. Lineage + DQ checks (great_expectations) + alerts on volume/freshness together give a fast root cause.
nodes.title: Lineage and data quality
